draft.title: Agonists, antagonists and stabilisers
card: the muscle that contracts to cause a movement. It is also called the prime mover.
the muscle that works against the agonist. It relaxes and lengthens to allow the movement to happen.
a muscle that holds other joints or body parts steady, so the agonist can pull from a firm base.
A muscle's role depends on the movement. In a bicep curl the biceps is the agonist and the triceps is the antagonist. When the arm straightens, the roles swap.
draft.remember: The agonist moves the joint, the antagonist relaxes to let it, and stabilisers keep the rest steady.

a.q: During a bicep curl, the triceps relaxes and lengthens. What is its role?
a.why: The triceps works against the biceps and relaxes to allow the elbow to bend, so it is the antagonist. It is not the agonist, because the biceps is the muscle that contracts to cause the bend.
a.clue: Which muscle allows the movement by relaxing?

b.q: Jess straightens her arm to push a ball away in a chest pass. Her triceps contracts to cause the elbow to straighten. What is the role of her biceps in this movement?
opts: Antagonist, as it relaxes to allow the arm to straighten
Agonist, as it is the muscle that crosses the elbow
Stabiliser, as it holds the elbow steady during the pass
Agonist, as it was the agonist in the bicep curl
b.why: The triceps is now the agonist, so the biceps is the antagonist and relaxes to allow the elbow to straighten. Roles depend on the movement, so the biceps being the agonist in a curl does not make it the agonist here.
b.clue: Which muscle is causing this movement, and what does the other one do?

b.best: Antagonist, as it relaxes to allow the arm to straighten
